lesson_title: The Line That Owes the Least: Regression
hook_text: Kids with bigger feet read better. Fact. So do big feet teach reading? The trap every data headline wants you to fall into.
clip_script: Measure every child in a primary school: shoe size and reading level. Plot the pairs — the dots climb in a beautiful straight lane, correlation near perfect. So big feet cause good reading? Obviously not — and THAT is the most important lesson in statistics. Age drives both: older children have bigger feet and read better, and the two columns merely march in step. Correlation is association, never proof of cause. Now the real machinery: six learners, practice papers versus marks. Lay a ruler through the dots — every dot bills you its vertical miss, the line that owes the least squared total is the regression line, and your calculator hands it over: 40,77 plus 3,83 x. Meaning: each paper buys about 3,83 more percentage points. Free check: the line always balances through the average point. And prediction has a fence — inside the observed range, trust it: five and a half papers, about sixty-two percent. Outside it, twenty papers promises 117 percent. Marks stop at a hundred. Jump the fence, flag the jump.
visual_style: A scatterplot building dot by dot, a ruler settling into the cloud with squared-gap tiles shrinking, a see-saw balancing at the mean point, and a warning fence at the edge of the data range.
mood: Myth-busting, sharp, the satisfying click of a trap avoided.
pacing: Hook on the shoe-size trap, a beat on the reveal, brisk through the ruler and the price of a paper, firm close at the fence.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never fall for a data headline again.
